name: Boston Dynamics
short_description: World leader in athletic legged robots with the Spot and Atlas platforms.
why_relevant: Defined what is physically possible in quadruped and humanoid robotics.
history: Founded in 1992 as a spin-off of MIT's Leg Lab, Boston Dynamics spent its early years solving fundamental problems of dynamic locomotion. Google acquired the company in 2013, followed by SoftBank in 2017, and Hyundai Motor Group took majority ownership in 2020. Its first commercial product, the Spot quadruped, launched in 2020 and has deployed thousands of units for industrial inspection, followed by Stretch for warehouse truck unloading. Today the Waltham-based firm continues pushing humanoid autonomy with the electric Atlas platform while expanding commercial offerings.

name: Figure AI
short_description: Developer of the Figure 01/02 general-purpose humanoid robot.
why_relevant: Commercial push for humanoids in logistics and manufacturing.
history: Founded in 2022 by entrepreneur Brett Adcock, Figure AI set out to commercialize general-purpose humanoids within a few years. In early 2024 it announced a landmark funding round, securing roughly $675 million at a $2.6 billion valuation from backers including Microsoft, OpenAI, NVIDIA, and Jeff Bezos, and unveiled the Figure 02 in August 2024. A BMW manufacturing partnership put early prototypes to work in the carmaker's South Carolina plant. In 2025 the company introduced Figure 03 with conversational AI and began piloting deployments with larger logistics clients.

name: Agility Robotics
short_description: Creator of Digit, a humanoid robot built for warehouse logistics.
why_relevant: First humanoids deployed in real logistics customer operations.
history: Agility Robotics was founded in 2015 as a spin-out from Oregon State University, where co-founder Jonathan Hurst's research underpinned the company's bipedal designs. The startup revealed its Digit humanoid in 2019 and spent the following years maturing the robot for warehouse labor. In 2022 it signed its first commercial deployments, including a landmark partnership with logistics giant GXO, and in 2023 opened its RoboFab 'Factory of the Future' in Salem, Oregon to mass-produce Digit. Agility now sells Digit commercially to fulfillment operators and continues iterating toward broader workplace autonomy.

name: Unitree Robotics
short_description: Builds quadrupeds and the G1 humanoid at consumer-affordable prices.
why_relevant: Brought legged robotics costs down dramatically worldwide.
history: Unitree Robotics was founded in Hangzhou in 2016 by Wang Xingxing, who began building low-cost quadruped robots while still a student. The company rapidly churned out a line of affordable legged machines, from the Go1 companion quadruped to the industrial-grade B2, undercutting Western rivals by a wide margin. Its humanoid push began with the H1 in 2023, followed by the compact $16,000 G1 in 2024 and the wheeled R1 in late 2024. Unitree has since shipped its platforms worldwide, positioning China at the center of affordable legged and humanoid robotics.

name: 1X Technologies
short_description: Developer of the NEO home humanoid with an OpenAI-backed vision.
why_relevant: Betting on software-driven humanoids for consumer environments.
history: Founded in 2014 as Halodi Robotics and renamed 1X Technologies in 2021, the Norwegian firm spent its first years engineering safe series-elastic actuators for service robots. Its wheeled humanoid EVE entered security and logistics trials across Europe and the United States, and in 2023 the company raised a significant round backed by OpenAI, signaling a bet on embodied AI. The NEO home humanoid was unveiled in 2024 as a soft, low-noise companion aimed at domestic environments. 1X is now scaling pilot deployments while training NEO on large-scale teleoperation data.

name: Sanctuary AI
short_description: Builds the Phoenix humanoid guided by a teleoperation-trained AI.
why_relevant: Combines human-in-the-loop training with general-purpose robots.
history: Sanctuary AI was founded in Vancouver in 2018 by a team led by Geordie Rose of D-Wave, aiming to build general-purpose humanoid workers on a foundation of human-in-the-loop learning. The company developed Carbon, a hydraulics-free platform, and unveiled its sixth-generation Phoenix humanoid in 2023. Early deployments paired human teleoperators with the robot to teach manipulation skills through demonstration rather than traditional programming. Rolling with a consistent cadence of hardware revisions, Sanctuary has since aligned with nearly 100 customer engagements and continues refining Carbon toward general-purpose autonomy.

name: Apptronik
short_description: Developer of Apollo, a humanoid designed for industrial shifts.
why_relevant: Partnered with major industries to move toward humanoid workforces.
history: Apptronik spun out of the University of Texas at Austin's Human Centered Robotics Lab in 2016 after helping build NASA's Valkyrie humanoid. The Austin-based company spent years developing industrial manipulators and exoskeleton research before unveiling its Apollo humanoid in August 2023. Freight and logistics operator GXO ordered a large initial batch, and Mercedes-Benz announced a pilot for the automotive assembly line. Backed by Garmin co-founder Min Kao, Apptronik is positioning Apollo as a tireless worker for dull, dirty, and dangerous jobs as humanoid adoption accelerates.

name: ANYbotics
short_description: Maker of ANYmal, an autonomous quadruped for industrial inspection.
why_relevant: Proved legged robots can replace humans in hazardous plant inspection.
history: ANYbotics was founded in 2016 as a spin-off of ETH Zurich, building on years of quadruped research led by co-founder Péter Fankhauser. Its ANYmal robot specialized in high-payload sensor autonomy, climbing stairs and navigating industrial plants independently. The company raised multiple growth rounds, most notably a $50 million Series B in 2023, and launched ANYmal X in 2024 for hazardous, explosive-rated inspection environments. Deployed with energy majors and industrial operators across Europe, ANYbotics now runs a structured rollout of autonomous aerial and ground inspection fleets.

name: Fourier Intelligence
short_description: Builds the GR humanoid series and rehabilitation exoskeletons.
why_relevant: Bridges clinical rehab robotics and general humanoids.
history: Fourier Intelligence was established in Singapore in 2015 to apply robotics to clinical rehabilitation. The company first developed and distributed rehabilitation exoskeletons and motion-therapy devices, building a network of partners across China and Southeast Asia. In 2023 it pivoted into the consumer and industrial humanoid market with the GR-1, a full-size general-purpose humanoid, followed by the GR-2 in 2024 with improved manipulation and touch capabilities. Fourier now balances its rehabilitative roots with an ambitious humanoid roadmap aimed at hospitals, services, and homes.

name: Skild AI
short_description: Builds a shared brain foundation model for embodied agents.
why_relevant: Argues robot skills should be a single learnable foundation model.
history: Skild AI was founded in 2023 by Carnegie Mellon alumni Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta, who met around the idea that robot capabilities should live in a single scalable model. The startup introduced Skild Brain, a robotics foundation model trained on broad multisensor data rather than task-specific demos. In 2024 it closed a $300 million Series A led by SoftBank Vision Fund and Lightspeed, valuing the company near $1.5 billion within about a year of founding. Skild is now adapting its brain across different robot bodies and driving toward generality in manipulation and locomotion tasks.

name: Physical Intelligence
short_description: Developer of the pi generalist robot foundation model.
why_relevant: Leading effort toward one model that controls many robots.
history: Physical Intelligence was founded in 2022 in San Francisco by robotics researchers including Karol Hausman, Sergey Levine, Chelsea Finn, and Brian Ichter, uniting talent from Google and Stanford. The company focuses on a generalist policy called pi, built on transformer-based world models that can control many different robots. In late 2024 it introduced pi-0, an open-vocabulary vision-language-action model, and secured roughly $400 million in funding at a reported $2.4 billion valuation. Early customer deployments include folding clothes for retailers, with the team pushing toward increasingly general embodied intelligence.

name: Intrinsic
short_description: Alphabet company building AI software to make industrial robots easier to use.
why_relevant: Attacks the cost of programming industrial robots.
history: Intrinsic emerged in 2021 as an independent Alphabet company, formed inside X's moonshot factory to make industrial robots easier to program. Led by CEO Wendy Tan White, it developed Flowstate, a software environment that lets engineers teach robot cells through perception-based building blocks rather than hand-written code. The company acquired Open Robotics, stewards of the ROS open-source robotics ecosystem, in 2022 to widen its developer reach. Since then Intrinsic has focused on perception-driven assemblies for small and mid-size manufacturers, steadily moving its software stack into early commercial production settings.

name: Bright Machines
short_description: Builds microfactories that combine robots and software for assembly.
why_relevant: Rebundles AI, vision and robots into a drop-in manufacturing cell.
history: Bright Machines was founded in 2018 by Amar Hanspal, a former co-CEO of Autodesk, to reshape manufacturing with software-defined robotic cells. Built from the industrial automation unit of electronics manufacturer Flex, the company develops microfactories combining machine vision, robots, and configuration software for high-mix assembly. It shipped systems to electronics and automotive customers and in 2025 closed a $226 million Series C led by NVIDIA, Microsoft, and Rockwell Automation, tripling its valuation to roughly $1.6 billion. Bright Machines now pairs its cell hardware with a cloud platform that reconfigures production lines purely in software.

name: Universal Robots
short_description: Inventor of the mass-market collaborative robot arm (cobot).
why_relevant: Created the ubiquitous cobot category, now part of Teradyne.
history: Universal Robots was founded in Odense, Denmark, in 2005 by Esben Østergaard, Kasper Støy, and Kristian Kassow, who set out to put collaborative robot arms within reach of small workshops. Its first UR5 cobot launched in 2008 with force-sensing joints and safety features that made fenced automation unnecessary. Teradyne acquired the company in 2015, accelerating global distribution. By 2023 Universal Robots had shipped more than 75,000 cobots worldwide and expanded into heavy-payload models, the UR20 and UR30, cementing its role as the pioneer of the mass-market cobot category.

name: Locus Robotics
short_description: Deploys fleets of autonomous mobile robots for warehouse fulfillment.
why_relevant: Proven multi-billion-unit throughput partner of major logistics firms.
history: Locus Robotics was founded in 2014 in Wilmington, Massachusetts, by veterans of fulfillment operator Quiet Logistics to solve warehouse labor shortages with fleets of autonomous mobile robots. Locus AMRs whisk carts through distribution centers while workers pick at stations, and the company signed marquee customers including DHL and Boots UK within its first years. It crossed more than 2 billion units picked cumulatively and topped $1 billion in lifetime customer orders, expanding across North America and the EU. The company also added Locus Vector, a high-throughput heavier-duty AMR, as e-commerce throughput demand surged.

name: Dexterity
short_description: Builds robotic systems for depalletizing and box handling in warehouses.
why_relevant: Reliable high-throughput case handling in real distribution centers.
history: Dexterity was founded in 2017 by Samir Menon, a Stanford-trained roboticist who previously worked within Google's robotics research efforts. The Redwood City company builds full systems for case depalletizing, induction, and truck unloading used by major retailers and parcel operators. Its vision-driven manipulation stack handles millions of boxes at scale, standing in for jobs that are notoriously hard to fill. Dexterity raised steady venture rounds during the warehouse-automation boom and today operates production deployments in distribution centers across North America, Japan, and Europe.

name: Covariant
short_description: Develops the RFM-1 foundation model for general robot manipulation.
why_relevant: Pioneered learning-from-data general grasping in logistics.
history: Covariant was founded in 2017 by UC Berkeley professor Pieter Abbeel and former OpenAI researchers, becoming the best-known brand in AI-powered warehouse grasping. Its Brains platform learned pick-and-place from real deployment data, and in 2024 the company unveiled RFM-1, a multimodal foundation model for robot manipulation. Amazon deployed hundreds of Covariant-powered arms across its fulfillment network, and in 2025 Amazon moved to acquire much of the company's foundation-model team, marking one of the largest exits in warehouse robotics to date.

name: Chef Robotics
short_description: Builds robots that assemble and plate food in high-volume kitchens.
why_relevant: Tackles the highest-turnover job category in food service.
history: Chef Robotics was founded in 2019 by Rajat Bhageria, applying computer vision and manipulators to food production lines where labor turnover is extreme. Its robots assemble ingredients onto bowls and plates, adapting to irregular natural products that frustrate traditional automation. The company counts major food manufacturers as customers and in 2024 raised a $43 million Series B led by Insight Partners. Chef Robotics has since doubled its deployments across meal-kit, protein, and prepared-foods facilities, with a roadmap toward full-kitchen automation.

name: Galbot
short_description: Builds wheeled humanoid robots for warehouse and retrieval tasks.
why_relevant: Strong material-handling deployment cadence in Chinese logistics.
history: Galbot was founded in Beijing in 2016 and spent its early years developing embodied AI and dual-arm manipulation for warehouse and retail scenarios. Its wheeled, humanoid-style platforms with vertically telescoping bodies are built for shelf picking, box handling, and last-yard retrieval in tight aisles. The company reached industrial maturity as Chinese logistics operators sought robots to relieve dock-to-shelf labor, and it now runs production deployments across logistics hubs. Galbot pairs Chinese-scale hardware with models trained on warehouse data, aiming for continuous material-handling autonomy in real distribution settings.

name: Clone Robotics
short_description: Builds humanoids with synthetic muscles and bones.
why_relevant: Radical actuator approach modeled on human musculoskeletal structure.
history: Clone Robotics was founded in 2021 in Wrocław, Poland, by a small team determined to rebuild human anatomy with synthetic materials rather than motors and gears. Drawing on soft-robotics research, the company developed myofibers, pneumatic artificial muscles that contract like biological tissue, and lavished them on a musculoskeletal humanoid skeleton. In 2024 Clone revealed the Alpha hand, a lifelike muscle-driven gripper, and followed with Protoclone V1, a full-body humanoid prototype. The company attracts investor attention by betting on tendon-driven, force-adaptive platforms that move with human-like fluidity.

name: Rainbow Robotics
short_description: Developer of the RB series humanoid, now backed by Samsung.
why_relevant: South Korea's flagship humanoid builder backed by Samsung.
history: Rainbow Robotics was founded in 2011 in Daejeon, South Korea, by engineers who helped build the HUBO humanoid at KAIST, home of the first bipedal robot to win the DARPA Robotics Challenge. The company commercialized its expertise through the RB series, shifting from logistics robots toward flexible humanoids with the RB-Y1, an arm-and-torso platform aimed at industrial manipulation. In late 2024 Samsung Electronics acquired roughly a 17 percent stake, becoming the largest shareholder and signaling the chaebol's humanoid ambitions. Rainbow now supplies dual-arm systems to manufacturers across Asia and the United States.

name: Xpeng Robotics
short_description: EV maker's robotics arm developing the Iron humanoid.
why_relevant: Ties EV-level engineering to humanoid manufacturing.
history: Xpeng Robotics was established in 2020 as the robotics arm of Chinese electric-vehicle maker XPeng, tapping the company's manufacturing and AI know-how. Its Iron humanoid was developed in-house to reuse automotive engineering, including smart-eye vision for spatial perception. During 2025 XPeng began deploying the prototype alongside roughly 300 workers in its manufacturing plants, gathering data for autonomous assembly tasks. The company is also running humanoid pilots in retail and service settings, betting that EV-grade sensing and compute give it an edge in the race toward physical AI.

name: Nuro
short_description: Builds the R2 curb-side delivery robot for local commerce.
why_relevant: Commercial curb-to-door robot delivery with major retail partners.
history: Nuro was founded in 2016 by former Waymo engineers Dave Ferguson and Jiajun Zhu to build purpose-built delivery robots without a driver cabin. Its road-legal R1 and R2 vehicles received state and federal approvals, and the company partnered with Kroger, Domino's, and Uber Eats for commercial deliveries. A $600 million round in 2021 valued Nuro near $8.6 billion, but a turbulent 2023 brought layoffs and a strengthened funding position. In 2024 Nuro unveiled a third-generation vehicle and re-emerged with retail-focused pilots and a licensing strategy around its L4 autonomy stack.

name: Serve Robotics
short_description: Operates self-driving sidewalk robots for food delivery.
why_relevant: Public Nasdaq company scaling robotic last-mile delivery.
history: Serve Robotics was created in 2021 after Uber spun off its Postmates delivery-robot team into an independent startup led by Ali Kashani. It went public on Nasdaq via a SPAC merger in 2022, becoming the first publicly traded sidewalk-delivery robot maker. Its robots serve food orders with partners like Uber Eats and Shake Shack. A 2024 raise that included NVIDIA deepened its AI integration and funded a target fleet of 2,000 robots. Serve now licenses its autonomy stack and expands to university and retail campuses, pressing toward profitability.

name: Cartken
short_description: Provides AI-driven sidewalk robots backed by major tech partners.
why_relevant: White-label autonomy for last-mile robot fleets.
history: Cartken was founded in 2019 in Oakland, California, by Christian Bersch and Anil Nanduri after they left Apple and Google, respectively. The company sells autonomy as a white-label service, letting delivery and mobility operators plug its perception stack into their own robots. Early deployments spanned university campuses, and a landmark 2022 partnership with Japan Post and Mitsubishi Electric brought Cartken robots to Tokyo streets. Backed by tech veterans, Cartken expanded into Asia through Alipay collaborations and now runs sidewalk fleets across Japan, the United States, and China.

name: Sarcos Technology
short_description: Develops powered exoskeletons and teleoperated robots for industry.
why_relevant: Ergonomic augmentation for physically demanding industrial jobs.
history: Sarcos Technology grew out of decades-long teleoperated-robot research at the University of Utah, with the company formally established around 2007 and headquartered in Salt Lake City. Its flagship Guardian XO is a powered full-body exoskeleton that amplifies human strength for industrial lifting, while its Guardian robots support inspection and manipulation in dangerous environments. The company went public through a SPAC merger in 2022 and later consolidated operations, narrowing focus on exoskeleton production and defense and aerospace applications to reach commercial scale with a more concentrated product line.

name: Ekso Bionics
short_description: Builds wearable exoskeletons for stroke rehab and mobility.
why_relevant: Evidence-based exoskeleton therapy used in hospitals.
history: Ekso Bionics traces its founding to 2005, when a group of engineers collaborating with UC Berkeley robotics professor Homayoon Kazerooni began producing exoskeletons and industrial assistance devices. The company pivoted to medical applications and won FDA clearance for its Ekso GT lower-limb exoskeleton for stroke and spinal cord rehabilitation, which is now used in hundreds of hospitals. Ekso went public on Nasdaq in 2014 and strengthened its therapy ecosystem with connected rehab reporting software. Today the Richmond, California company continues expanding clinical evidence across stroke, spinal injury, and mobility conditions.

name: Mujin
short_description: Develops controller technology enabling mixed-lot robotic depalletizing.
why_relevant: Sells a universal brain for hard industrial motion tasks.
history: Mujin was founded in Tokyo in 2011 by Issei Takino and Rosen Diankov, who developed a universal motion-planning controller for fleets of hard industrial robots. Its MujinController provides motion planning, calibration, and machine vision that lets manipulators handle mixed loads without per-installation programming. The company scaled deployments in logistics, automotive, and consumer goods across Japan, China, and the United States. In 2025 consultancy Accenture acquired Mujin to anchor its push into intelligent manufacturing and robotic depalletization at industrial scale.

name: Clearpath Robotics
short_description: Maker of the Otto line of autonomous industrial vehicles.
why_relevant: Canada's answer to heavy-load autonomous material transport.
history: Clearpath Robotics was founded in 2009 in Kitchener, Ontario, by University of Waterloo engineering graduates Matt Rendall, Bryan Webb, and Ryan Gariepy. The company started with research platforms like Husky and Jackal for universities and labs, then launched its Otto line of heavy-duty autonomous mobile robots for factory logistics. With deployments in automotive and consumer-goods plants worldwide, Clearpath became a leading Western AMR supplier. In 2023 Rockwell Automation acquired the company to fold its autonomy stack into an industrial automation portfolio, and Otto robots continue serving manufacturing customers globally.

name: Vention
short_description: Platform to design, simulate and deploy robotic workcells in one day.
why_relevant: Brings no-code configuration to industrial automation.
history: Vention was founded in Montreal in 2016 by Etienne Lacroix to make industrial automation approachable for engineers of all skill levels. Its MachineBuilder platform lets users drag, drop, and simulate robotic workcells from a catalog of components, then order and assemble the machine within days. The platform attracted strong traction among mid-size manufacturers during the automation boom, and the company raised a Series C led by Bessemer Venture Partners in 2023. Vention has since grown a network of partner integrators and expanded its cloud robotics software to run the very cells it helps design.
